number_of_offences: Multiple offences/counts charged, but only one was finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The FSL report was one of the evidences collected by I.O. Its evidentiary value was still to be gone into at the time of trial in the light of the evidences, which may come before the trial court.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the opinion of a handwriting expert is only opinion evidence, which is a weak nature of evidence and could not have been relied in rejecting the claim of the appellant that he has opened the account in exercise of his official duty.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 14.11.2000; Trial judgment: 13.12.2014; High Court decision: 06.08.2018; Supreme Court decision: APRIL 30, 2019
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Ajayinder Sangwan, Rajkumar Sharma, V.P. Singh, T.P. Singh, Sachin Choudhary, Summinder Paswan, Pradeep Kumar Sharma, Amuridh Kumar, Devendra Singh, Advs. Counsel for the State: V. Balaji, Nachiketa Joshi, Praneet Pranav, B.V. Balaram Das, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Application dismissed; High Court: Application dismissed; Supreme Court: Appeal partly allowed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant, being a public servant, required sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. for prosecution, and that the CMM's rejection of the discharge application was correct. They also emphasized that the alleged acts of forgery were not in the discharge of official duty.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant was not a public servant removable from his office with the sanction of the Government, thus Section 197 Cr.P.C. did not apply. They also contended that the CMM's opinion on forgery was premature and that the handwriting expert's opinion was weak and not conclusive.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that Section 197 Cr.P.C. applies only to public servants not removable from their office save by or with the sanction of the Government. The Court also emphasized that a Magistrate should avoid making conclusive opinions on evidence prior to trial.
precedent_relied_upon: K.CH. Prasad v. Smt. J. Vanalatha Devi and Others (1987) 2 SCC 52; Parkash Singh Badal and Another v. State of Punjab and Others (2007) 1 SCC 1; S.P.S. Rathore v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another (2017) 5 SCC 817; Inspector of Police and Another v. Battenapatla Venkata Ratnam and Another (2015) 13 SCC 87; Devinder Singh and Others v. State of Punjab (2016) 12 SCC 87; N. K. Ganguly v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2016) 2 SCC 143
